comments.author: Alexander Terp
comments.body:
Done, and it answered more than it was asked. corpus/herdr-0.8.0/layout
holds five panes at three levels with a split under each side of the
root, plus zoom, a divider drag, a close, and a crowding sweep to
sixteen panes. Findings in observations section 13.

Where geometry comes from is settled: layout_updated. Every split in
the exported tree has a border in the snapshot covering exactly the
panes beneath it, same direction and ratio, so structure is
reconstructible from the live event with no second request. The border
ids independently spell the same paths (split_2_01 = first, second),
and layout.set_split_ratio takes that same path - so rebuilding the
tree also derives the address a divider drag is sent back on.

Two things that would have bitten later. The rects are about nobody's
window: the area is a fixed 54x23 whether a client is attached at
200x50 or not attached at all, so only structure and ratios transfer.
And zoom leaves every pane listed at its unzoomed rect with only a
flag moving, so a view that renders what it is given paints every pane
while the daemon shows one.

The crowding sweep was the one that could have gone badly. It did not:
at sixteen panes every covering rect was still distinct, smallest
dimension 5 cells.

creator: Alexander Terp
description:
Chunk E cannot be planned against the corpus as it stands: the deepest recorded layout is three panes at two levels, captured as a side effect of the lifecycle scenario. Deciding where geometry comes from - session.snapshot rects, layout.export's BSP tree, or a reconstruction - needs a recording with mixed directions and real nesting to check any design against.

Blocks a_26BJGL7VZ more than it looks: a design checked against one split level is a design checked against nothing.
title: 🌲 Record a nested layout deeper than one split
